items.title: Evaluating AI-Driven Speech Recognition Tools for Pronunciation Training Among EFL Learners
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence driven speech recognition is increasingly used to support pronunciation practice in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, yet less attention has been given to how learners experience and interpret automated feedback during actual learning activities. This study examined EFL learners’ experiences with AI driven speech recognition for pronunciation training, focusing on feedback usefulness, recognition limitations, changes in learning strategies, and teacher mediation. A qualitative interpretive design was employed with undergraduate EFL learners who engaged in pronunciation activities supported by an AI driven speech recognition tool. Data were collected through semi structured interviews, classroom observations, learner reflection logs, and digital learning artifacts and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that learners valued immediate feedback because it enabled repeated practice, self monitoring, and independent correction. However, recognition inconsistencies sometimes made it difficult to determine whether unsuccessful evaluations reflected pronunciation problems or system limitations. Learners therefore interpreted automated feedback critically rather than accepting it as an unquestionable judgment. The findings further indicated that AI supported learner agency, while teacher mediation remained important for clarifying ambiguous feedback and guiding pronunciation adjustments. The study concludes that AI driven speech recognition is most useful as a complementary resource within teacher supported pronunciation instruction, with its pedagogical value depending on both recognition capability and learners’ ability to interpret and use feedback strategically.

items.title: Facilitating Reflection Using AI-Generated Visual Representations of Metaphors
items.abstract: Reflection plays a crucial role in self-directed learning (SDL), enabling learners to connect past experiences, understand present actions, and set future goals. Metaphors can support this reflective process by offering a way to conceptualize learning that may be difficult to express directly, particularly when affective dimensions are involved. As generative AI has become prevalent in educational settings, its application has been increasingly explored. However, research on AI use for supporting learners’ reflective processes in SDL remains limited. This study therefore investigated students’ experiences with a metaphor-based reflection activity that incorporates an AI text-to-image generator. Participants were 24 Japanese university students who engaged in SDL through Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). They created metaphors representing their SDL experiences and used OpenArt, a free online artificial intelligence (AI) text-to-image model, to generate visual representations. Data were collected through open-ended questionnaire items and analyzed using frequency counts and thematic analysis. Findings showed that AI-generated visual metaphors may provide an additional resource for reflective practice, while highlighting the need for scaffolding in metaphor creation, prompt writing, and critical evaluation of AI-generated representations. The study offers implications for educators exploring GenAI as a resource for promoting reflection.

items.title: Factors that Affect Customer Trust with Intent Using Veronika's Generative-Based Chatbot on Providers Telecommunications
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed customer service interactions, including Telkomsel’s implementation of the Veronika chatbot as a digital service solution. However, maintaining customer trust and continued usage intention remains challenging because of variations in information accuracy, usability, and perceived benefits. This study examines the effects of chatbot information quality on perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, customer trust, and continued usage intention toward Veronika, Telkomsel’s generative AI-based chatbot. This study employed a quantitative approach using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 397 Telkomsel customers who had interacted with the chatbot. The findings indicate that chatbot information quality significantly affects perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, which, in turn, increase customer trust. Furthermore, trust plays a significant role in determining users’ intention to continue using Veronika. The results also demonstrate that perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and trust mediate the relationship between information quality and continued usage intention. These findings imply that improving the accuracy, relevance, and responsiveness of chatbot information, as well as the chatbot’s usability, is essential for strengthening customer trust and encouraging the sustained adoption of AI-based customer service platforms.

items.title: From Perception to Prevention: Preserving Safety-Signal Integrity Across Cognitive and Organisational Gaps in Near-Miss Learning
items.abstract: Near-miss reporting is an important component of proactive safety management, yet the reliability of near-miss information depends on more than the availability of reporting systems. This Perspective argues that a critical but often overlooked source of information loss occurs between hazard experience, perception, recognition, and reporting. Safety systems frequently assume that workers consistently recognise and classify hazardous events, although human perception is influenced by experience, familiarity, attention, task context, and the visibility and complexity of hazards. Consequently, some safety-significant experiences may remain unrecognised, while others may be recognised but not reported, limiting the completeness of near-miss information used for prevention. Drawing on safety science, human factors, and occupational psychology, this Perspective conceptualises near-miss reporting as an information pathway in which cognitive and organisational gaps can progressively reduce safety-signal visibility. It highlights the importance of context-based hazard-recognition training, accessible reporting mechanisms, and organisational conditions that enable workers to convert safety experiences into usable information. The article proposes a perception-to-prevention perspective in which improving the integrity of safety signals requires connecting human recognition with inclusive reporting and organisational learning.

items.title: From Understanding to Collaboration: Unpacking the Black Box of Collaboration Between Street-Level Bureaucrats and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Street-level bureaucrats (SLBs) increasingly collaborate with artificial intelligence (AI), yet research on human-AI collaboration (HAIC) lacks evidence from public organizations. This study examines the association between SLBs’ understanding of AI and their AI collaboration, based on a department-level census of 175 SLBs in Hangzhou, where SLB-AI collaboration occupies a leading position in China. The key findings are as follows. (1) Based on respondents’ evaluations, SLB-AI collaboration is perceived to outperform both SLB-only and AI-only modes in work efficiency, but it does not significantly surpass SLB-only mode in emotional competence. (2) SLBs’ understanding of AI is positively associated with collaboration and serves as an enabling condition for it. (3) The relationship between understanding and collaboration is significant under low-to-moderate work stress, but not under high work stress. These findings open the black box of SLB-AI collaboration in public organizations, highlighting the need for human-centered SLB-AI discretion and bureaucratic systems.

items.title: Humble leadership and employee self-development in SMEs: a four-wave multilevel study of job autonomy and intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Abstract Background Employee self-development is important for workers to update their skills and respond to changing work environments. However, less is known about how humble leadership is positively associated with self-development through employees’ psychological experiences. Drawing on social information processing theory and the job demands-resources perspective, this study examines whether team-level humble leadership is positively associated with individual self-development through job autonomy and intrinsic motivation. Methods A four-wave survey was conducted among employees from small and medium-sized enterprises in Shandong Province, China. The final sample included 368 employees nested in 83 teams. Humble leadership was measured at Time 1, job autonomy at Time 2, intrinsic motivation at Time 3, and self-development at Time 4. Multilevel structural equation modeling in Mplus was used to test the hypotheses. Confidence intervals estimated in Mplus were used to examine the indirect effects. Results At the between level, humble leadership was positively related to employee self-development, job autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. At the within level, job autonomy and intrinsic motivation were positively related to self-development. Job autonomy was also positively related to intrinsic motivation at both the within and between levels. The sequential indirect effect of humble leadership on self-development through job autonomy and intrinsic motivation was significant. The indirect effect through job autonomy alone was not significant. Conclusions The findings suggest that humble leadership is positively associated with employee self-development through employees’ perceived job autonomy and intrinsic motivation. Job autonomy may provide room for self-development, but it may not be enough by itself in a cross-level process. Employees are more likely to use autonomy for sustained self-development when autonomy is linked to intrinsic motivation. This study highlights a multilevel psychological mechanism linking humble leadership to employee self-development in SMEs.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems
items.abstract: Multi-hazard early warning systems are increasingly central to disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation, yet their effectiveness depends on more than forecast accuracy. Artificial intelligence is expanding capabilities in risk mapping, environmental monitoring, forecasting, impact estimation, communication, and decision support. The emerging literature, however, already demonstrates that artificial intelligence can contribute across the established early-warning pillars; repeating that proposition offers limited conceptual novelty. This review therefore shifts attention from individual components to the quality of the information transformations that connect them. Drawing on a focused integrative review of recent peer-reviewed scholarship and authoritative international guidance, the paper introduces handoff integrity as a conceptual construct for artificial-intelligence-enabled multi-hazard early warning systems. Handoff integrity denotes the extent to which risk information remains or becomes contextually meaningful, timely, uncertainty-aware, interpretable, actionable, accountable, and accessible as it crosses functional and institutional boundaries. The framework identifies five critical handoffs: risk contextualization, forecast-to-impact translation, impact-to-warning translation, warning-to-action orchestration, and response-to-learning feedback. Six dimensions - semantic fidelity, contextual relevance, timeliness, uncertainty traceability, actionability, and accountability and inclusiveness - provide a basis for evaluating these interfaces. The framework positions artificial intelligence as an integration layer rather than an autonomous substitute for scientific institutions, emergency authorities, local knowledge, or human judgment. It further identifies data interoperability, governance, equity, trust, cybersecurity, institutional capacity, and lifecycle sustainability as conditions for durable performance. The paper contributes a technology-neutral, testable framework that extends evaluation beyond algorithmic accuracy toward the integrity of the pathway from risk knowledge to protective action.

items.abstract: Immersive technologies offer new possibilities for cultural heritage, yet their potential to foster social interaction, emotional connections, and cultural identity at cognate heritage sites remains underexplored. Based on Interaction Ritual Chain (IRC) theory, this study developed an emotional design model translating “co-presence,” “mutual focus,” and “shared emotion” into immersive interaction strategies. Using the Beijing and Xi'an Drum Towers as cases, we developed the “Resonance of Bells and Drums” system and evaluated it through a between-subjects experiment. Results showed the proposed model significantly outperformed the control condition in emotional energy, cultural identity, and behavioral intentions, demonstrating its effectiveness in fostering cross-regional emotional connections. The ablation conditions further revealed patterns of association between different design modules and immediate experiential and delayed outcomes. This study provides empirical support for applying IRC theory to digital heritage design and offers a reusable model for cognate cultural heritage dissemination.

items.title: Investigating Human--AI Discrepancies via Multiple-Solution Problems
items.abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models are benchmarked on whether they reach a correct answer. Yet many problems admit several correct answers and repeated attempts, by different people or by the same model resampled, trace out a distribution over them. In this work, we ask whether human and model reasoning lead to different distributions over valid solutions. Our testbed comprises 270 reasoning puzzles across five puzzle families. These multiple-solution puzzles each have 3 to 8 valid solutions and are simple enough that humans and models can solve them reliably. The resulting distributions differ markedly: models differ from one another, yet resemble each other far more than they resemble humans. Model distributions are, moreover, within every puzzle family, less diverse than human ones. We compare these discrepancies across puzzle categories, and trace how they respond to reasoning-effort settings, to prompting, and to perturbations of the puzzle that leave its solutions unchanged. Together, these results point at significant differences between human and AI problem-solving processes, and their choice among equally defensible solutions. As progressive deployment of AI systems in society comes into focus, evaluating such differences (beyond one-dimensional accuracy metrics) is increasingly important. Data and code are available at https://hai-discrepancies.github.io/

items.title: KITA AI: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Pluralistic Policy Deliberation
items.abstract: Public policies addressing urgent social and environmental challenges need to explicitly consider the diverse, often conflicting perspectives of the affected stakeholders. Despite computational decision-support approaches increasingly offering recommendations across diverse human value systems, they still tend to deliver a single consensus-driven outcome. We present KITA AI, a modular system in which multiple large language model agents, each grounded in distinct demographic stakeholder personas and conceptual frameworks, deliberate on policy scenarios. The objective of KITA AI is not merely to inform about a preferred policy proposal, but also to automatically surface who is affected by the scenario and provide decision-makers with the rationales and quantitative indicators behind each position. KITA AI treats non-convergence as a first-class explainable output, enabling policymakers to better understand the trade-offs and human impacts of the policies being discussed.

items.title: Learning to Optimize through Solver-Grounded Self-Play
items.abstract: Optimization modeling is central to many decision-making scenarios, but traditionally requires extensive domain expertise. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating this process, current training paradigms mainly rely on human-annotated or teacher-generated datasets. This dependence introduces a Generalization Ceiling, where models overfit to narrow data distributions, and Capability Anchoring, where models' reasoning is bounded by annotator proficiency and teacher model capability. In response, we propose OPT-Zero, the first fully self-play training framework for optimization modeling that requires zero external training data. OPT-Zero employs a single LLM in a dual-role closed loop: a Proposer that synthesizes increasingly challenging optimization problems alongside their mathematical formulations and solving code, and a Solver that attempts to resolve the problems given only natural-language problem descriptions. Grounded in execution feedback from external optimization solvers, we alternately train both roles using reinforcement learning. This process fosters an auto-curriculum in which the Proposer and Solver co-evolve: generating harder valid problems by the Proposer seamlessly enhances the structural reasoning ability of the Solver. Extensive results indicate that with zero curated data, OPT-Zero matches state-of-the-art data-dependent methods while exhibiting substantially stronger generalizability, establishing self-play training as a highly scalable paradigm for advancing LLM reasoning in modeling and solving optimization problems.

items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: A Framework for Reflective AI Use in Software Engineering Education
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in software engineering education, supporting activities such as requirements development, design exploration, documentation, and prototyping. However, educators often have visibility only into final artefacts, with limited insight into how students evaluate, verify, and refine AI-generated outputs during the learning process. This creates challenges for assessing evaluative judgement and responsible AI-assisted practice. This paper introduces the AI Journal, a structured reflection framework designed to make student-GenAI interaction visible in first-year software engineering education. The framework combines execution tracking, which records prompts, outputs, intent, and interaction context, with cognitive auditing, which captures verification strategies, intervention decisions, confidence judgements, critical learning moments, and reflections on AI-supported work. Deployed in a first-semester software engineering course, the AI Journal enabled visibility into aspects of student learning not observable through artefact-based assessments alone. Preliminary observations suggested variation in verification practices, intervention strategies, and perceptions of AI-supported work. Critical learning moments frequently occurred when students evaluated contextual suitability, feasibility, and requirements alignment rather than identifying obvious errors. The AI Journal demonstrates a practical, lightweight, and model-agnostic approach for making AI-assisted learning processes visible. By foregrounding verification, intervention, and reflection, it shifts attention from product-focused assessment toward evaluative judgement and responsible AI-assisted practice.

items.title: Navigating Artificial Intelligence in Neuroregulation Practice: Ethical Principles, Risk Stratification, and a Clinical Policy Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are entering neuroregulation practice through multiple simultaneous pathways, including automated qEEG analysis, protocol recommendation systems, AI-assisted documentation, and consumer-facing mental health applications that clients bring directly into the therapeutic relationship. No ethics code specific to neuroregulation has yet addressed these applications directly. This article presents a conceptual and practical ethical framework grounded in established codes, including the BCIA Code of Ethics, ISNR Code of Ethics, APA Ethical Principles, ACA Code of Ethics, and the APA (2025) Ethical Guidance for Artificial Intelligence. A risk continuum model organizing AI applications along three dimensions (opacity, clinical consequence, and distance from oversight) is proposed. Four ethical domains are addressed: informed consent and transparency, practitioner competence and scope, data privacy and vendor accountability, and three AI accuracy risks (hallucination, automation bias, and collusion). A five-element practice policy framework is presented in tabular form for direct clinical use. Existing ethics principles are sufficient to guide responsible AI integration when applied deliberately. The practitioner remains accountable for AI-assisted decisions regardless of tool design or vendor claims. Proactive policy development positions neuroregulation clinicians to shape the field's emerging standards.

items.title: Navigating Digital Transformation: Sociological and Educational Factors in Corporate AI Strategy Adoption
items.abstract: To address the practical challenge of the disconnect between AI strategy implementation and performance outcomes in enterprises, this study focuses on the three-dimensional execution mechanism encompassing "resourcesprocess-culture," examining its mediating role between AI strategies and corporate performance, as well as the moderating effects of firm size and industry characteristics. Data were collected via random sampling using the Wenjuanxing online survey platform, supplemented by a 12-month longitudinal case tracking study. Empirical analysis employed structural equation modeling, grouped regression, and interaction term testing. Results demonstrate that the three-dimensional execution mechanism fully mediates the relationship between AI strategies and corporate performance, with resource allocation playing the most significant mediating role. Firm size positively moderates the performance effect of the execution mechanism, with large firms exhibiting significantly better implementation outcomes than small and medium-sized enterprises. Industry characteristics exhibit heterogeneity: technology-intensive industries show stronger positive impacts of the execution mechanism compared to non-technology-intensive sectors. Differentiation in implementation pathways reveals adaptability— technology-intensive firms benefit from a "resource priority or lightweight resources plus cultural guidance" approach, while non-technology-intensive firms are better suited for a "culture priority plus lightweight processes" model. This study evaluates AI strategy implementation primarily through organizational financial and innovation performance indicators. Although these metrics serve as organizational-level proxies for implementation effectiveness, they do not directly measure employee-level social outcomes, such as workplace learning, well-being, psychological safety, re-skilling, or perceived equity; therefore, the social implications discussed in this study should be interpreted within this scope.

items.title: Online questionnaires as a pedagogical tool for enhancing student engagement in philosophy courses
items.abstract: The study aims to substantiate the methodological potential of online questionnaires as a pedagogical tool for increasing student engagement in the study of philosophy. The article examines the essence of the academic engagement phenomenon, paying particular attention to emotional-cognitive engagement, which presupposes the student’s personal involvement; demonstrates the significance of online questionnaires as an auxiliary tool when employing interactive teaching methods. The scientific novelty lies in substantiating the necessity of teaching philosophy based on the theory of academic engagement, while demonstrating that online surveys serve as a factor in boosting students’ emotional-cognitive engagement. The study analyzes the experience of conducting an online survey on the philosophy of artificial intelligence, organized by the authors in the 2025/26 academic year among students and postgraduate students of Kazan State University of Architecture and Engineering. Drawing on the survey data, the paper demonstrates that online questionnaires – traditionally used for diagnostic purposes – can also function as an effective pedagogical tool that, firstly, introduces an element of interactivity into the classroom; secondly, helps vividly reveal the “personal dimension” of abstract philosophical questions; and thirdly, increases students’ engagement in the educational process.

items.title: Polycentric risk governance across safety and security risk logics
items.abstract: The regulatory regime governing the Norwegian petroleum sector changed significantly in response to new geopolitical conditions following the war in Ukraine and the sabotage of the Nord Stream I and II pipelines. New legal security requirements and security risk logics were introduced into a sector whose traditional regulatory regime and risk logic had been intrinsically oriented toward safety. This shift altered the balance between safety and security considerations within the sector. This article explores the implications for regulatory regimes and risk logics when transitioning from safety-oriented to security-oriented regulatory models. Our ambition is primarily conceptual and theoretical, with the Norwegian petroleum industry serving as an illustrative case. The article analyses the emerging interface between safety and security, emphasizing the ontological, epistemological, and procedural divergences that complicate the integration of security concerns − focused on intentional, adversarial threats − into established safety regimes that manage unintentional harm. Anchored in a polycentric governance framework, the article examines how geopolitical developments have created tensions between rule-based and risk-based regulatory models, and the implications for organizational practices, regulatory oversight, and tripartite cooperation. It concludes by proposing a model of enforced self-regulation that reconciles safety and security logics, highlighting the need for adaptive, resilient, and knowledge-driven approaches to risk management in complex and evolving threat landscapes.

items.title: Predicting team success with quantitative metrics of communication patterns
items.abstract: This study introduces a communication coding scheme that captures team progress. Two new metrics, the disengagement ratio and forward index, are introduced and prove effective for distinguishing high and low performing teams. Forty-eight participants completed a communication-intensive game as defuser (operator). Transcripts were coded using speech act, speech category, and progress coding schemes. The disengagement ratio indexed reactivity versus initiative, while the forward index quantified communication that moved the task forward. Mixed-effects models showed that poor-performing teams made more information requests and repairs and had higher modified anticipation and disengagement ratios. Higher-performing teams showed a higher forward index and lower sideways frequency rate. The new disengagement and task-progress metrics capture additional dimensions of communication, and our findings indicate their potential for assessing team performance.Practitioner Summary Team performance depends on active, progress-oriented communication. The disengagement ratio and forward index distinguish high- and low-performing teams.
